slides.say: k, a, b and c are integers. Given: two k plus one is equal to a cubed, times b plus one, squared, times c minus five, to the power of four. Which of the numbers k, a, b, c is necessarily odd?
It looks scary, but it's one rule about odd products. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with that rule, and then plugging in numbers.

[short pause] Let's start with the left side, two k plus one. Two k is always even, and plus one makes it odd. k is two gives five, and k is three gives seven, both odd. So k can be anything, and the left side is odd.
So the right side is odd too. And a product is odd only when every factor is odd, because one even factor brings a two in. The powers don't matter, so let's go factor by factor.
a cubed is odd, so a is odd. b plus one is odd, so b is even. c minus five is odd, so c is even. Only a is necessarily odd, choice number two is our answer.
at: choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's try plugging in, and look for an example where k, b and c are even. a is one, b is zero, and c is six. One cubed is one, zero plus one is one, and six minus five is one. So the right side is one.
at: a is one, b is zero

slides.say: Two k plus one is one, so k is zero. And k, b and c are all even here, so choice numbers one, three and four are out. Choice number two. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: Two k plus one is one
